claim: A cage-shaped F-actin network is essential for maintaining a tight spatial organization of Cav1.3 Ca2+ channels at the synaptic ribbons of auditory inner hair cells.
source: We show that a cage-shaped F-actin network is essential for maintaining a tight spatial organization of Cav1.3 Ca2+ channels at the synaptic ribbons of auditory inner hair cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that latrunculin-A treatment disrupts F-actin cages and increases the distance between Cav1.3 and ribbons (Figure 1C, D).

claim: The F-actin network provides mechanosensitivity to the Cav1.3 channels when varying intracellular hydrostatic pressure.
source: This F-actin network is also found to provide mechanosensitivity to the Cav1.3 channels when varying intracellular hydrostatic pressure.
evidence: Supported by data showing that hydrostatic pressure effects on Ca2+ currents were no longer visible when IHCs were pre-treated with latrunculin-A (Figure 2A).

claim: The F-actin mesh network attached to the synaptic ribbons directly influences the efficiency of otoferlin-dependent exocytosis independently of its action on the Cav1.3 channels.
source: Furthermore, this F-actin mesh network attached to the synaptic ribbons directly influences the efficiency of otoferlin-dependent exocytosis and its sensitivity to intracellular hydrostatic pressure, independently of its action on the Cav1.3 channels.
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ uncaging experiments showing facilitation of exocytosis after latrunculin-A treatment, independent of Ca2+ channel activation (Figure 2C, D).

claim: The rate of vesicle recruitment to the ribbons is directly controlled by a synaptic F-actin network and changes in intracellular hydrostatic pressure.
source: We propose a new mechanistic model for vesicle exocytosis in auditory hair cells where the rate of vesicle recruitment to the ribbons is directly controlled by a synaptic F-actin network and changes in intracellular hydrostatic pressure.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data showing effects of F-actin disruption and hydrostatic pressure on exocytosis.

claim: Auditory hair cells convert tiny variations of sound pressure through the displacement of their apical hair bundles into analogous voltage waveforms.
source: Auditory hair cells convert tiny variations of sound pressure through the displacement of their apical hair bundles into analogous voltage waveforms.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about auditory hair cell function.

claim: Neural encoding of microphonic potentials occurs at the ribbon synapses of inner hair cells by mechanisms involving Cav1.3 channels.
source: Neural encoding of these microphonic potentials occurs at the ribbon synapses of inner hair cells (IHCs) by mechanisms involving Cav1.3 channels (Platzer et al., 2000; Brandt et al., 2003; Brandt et al., 2005) and otoferlin-dependent exocytosis of synaptic vesicles (Roux et al., 2006; Beurg et al., 2010, Vincent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neural encoding of microphonic potentials occurs at the ribbon synapses of inner hair cells by mechanisms involving otoferlin-dependent exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
source: Neural encoding of these microphonic potentials occurs at the ribbon synapses of inner hair cells (IHCs) by mechanisms involving Cav1.3 channels (Platzer et al., 2000; Brandt et al., 2003; Brandt et al., 2005) and otoferlin-dependent exocytosis of synaptic vesicles (Roux et al., 2006; Beurg et al., 2010, Vincent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IHCs have the extraordinary property to sustain indefatigably high rates of exocytosis during continuous sound stimulation.
source: Unlike most neuronal central synapses, IHCs have the extraordinary property to sustain indefatigably high rates of exocytosis during continuous sound stimulation (Safieddine et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The precise molecular mechanisms underlying fast and massive recruitment of synaptic vesicles to the IHC ribbon active zones remain elusive.
source: The precise molecular mechanisms underlying this fast and massive recruitment of synaptic vesicles to the IHC ribbon active zones still remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: An unconventional molecular regulation of synaptic vesicle fusion and replenishment of the releasable pool of vesicles has been proposed for IHCs.
source: The implication of an unconventional molecular regulation of synaptic vesicle fusion and replenishment of the releasable pool of vesicles has been proposed (Nouvian et al., 2011; Vogl et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In neuroendocrine cells, a network of sub-membranous cortical F-actin tightly regulates plasma membrane tension and the access of granules to secretory sites.
source: In other secretory cells such as neuroendocrine cells, a network of sub-membranous cortical F-actin is known to influence exocytosis greatly by tightly regulating plasma membrane tension and the access of the granules to the secretory sites (Apodaca, 2002; Torregrosa-Hetland et al., 2011; Gutierrez and Gil, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In central neuronal synapses, F-actin is involved in maintaining vesicle pools and regulating vesicle mobility.
source: In central neuronal synapses, F-actin is also involved in maintaining vesicle pools and regulating vesicle mobility (Cingolani and Goda, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Electron-tomography evidence for F-actin and microtubules near the synaptic ribbons has been observed in bullfrog hair cells.
source: Electron-tomography evidence for F-actin and microtubules near the synaptic ribbons has been observed in bullfrog hair cells (Graydon et al 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Whether IHC synaptic exocytosis is modulated by F-actin remains unknown.
source: Whether IHC synaptic exocytosis is modulated by F-actin remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: Hydrostatic pressure across the membrane influences exocytosis in mast cells.
source: Other factors affecting membrane tension and exocytosis in many cell types, such as mast cells, include hydrostatic pressure across the membrane (Solsona et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Hydrostatic pressure influences the spontaneous and evoked activity of vestibular hair cells of the dogfish by mechanisms that remain unknown.
source: This latter factor has also been shown to influence the spontaneous and evoked activity of vestibular hair cells of the dogfish by mechanisms that remain unknown (Fraser and Shelmerdine, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A dense F-actin network surrounds the IHC ribbon synaptic zones.
source: Direct labeling of F-actin with fluorescent phalloidin revealed the presence of a dense F-actin network that surrounded the IHC ribbon synaptic zones (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by direct experimental observation using fluorescent phalloidin labeling and confocal imaging.

claim: The F-actin network extends underneath the plasma membrane and forms intracellular dense cages beneath the synaptic ribbons.
source: This network extended underneath the plasma membrane and formed intracellular dense cages beneath the synaptic ribbons.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: F-actin cages display a mean size diameter of 0.8 ± 0.1 µm.
source: These cages displayed a mean size diameter of 0.8 ± 0.1 µm (n = 186 actives zones; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements from confocal imaging data.

claim: Each F-actin cage is generally associated with one ribbon and one Cav1.3 co-immunoreactive patch.
source: Overlapping with otoferlin, each F-actin cage was generally associated with one ribbon and one Cav1.3 co-immunoreactive patch.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ca2+ channels and the secretory machinery are associated with the borders of F-actin cytoskeletal cages in chromaffin cells.
source: Similarly, Ca2+ channels and the secretory machinery have been shown to be associated with the borders of F-actin cytoskeletal cages in chromaffin cells (Torregrosa-Hetland et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A 45-min treatment with 1 µM extracellular latrunculin-A completely disorganizes the synaptic F-actin cages in IHCs.
source: A 45-min treatment of the organ of Corti in vitro with 1 µM extracellular latrunculin-A completely disorganized the synaptic F-actin cages and the Cav1.3 immunoreactive-patches at the IHC ribbons (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data showing disrupted F-actin cages after latrunculin-A treatment.

claim: A 45-min treatment with 1 µM extracellular latrunculin-A completely disorganizes the Cav1.3 immunoreactive-patches at the IHC ribbons.
source: A 45-min treatment of the organ of Corti in vitro with 1 µM extracellular latrunculin-A completely disorganized the synaptic F-actin cages and the Cav1.3 immunoreactive-patches at the IHC ribbons (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data showing disrupted Cav1.3 patches after latrunculin-A treatment.

claim: The mean distance between the Cav1.3 immunoreactive patches and the ribbons increases from 218 ± 11 nm in controls to 260 ± 12 nm with latrunculin-A treatment.
source: The mean distance between the Cav1.3 immunoreactive patches and the ribbons increased from 218 ± 11 nm (n = 71) in controls to 260 ± 12 nm with latrunculin-A treatment (n = 102; p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements from confocal imaging data.

claim: Latrunculin-A treatment facilitates exocytosis in IHCs compared to controls while voltage-gated Ca2+ currents remain unchanged.
source: In the latter conditions, surprisingly, whole-cell patch clamp recordings revealed a largely facilitated exocytosis as compared to controls, while voltage-gated Ca2+ currents were unchanged (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing increased exocytosis without changes in Ca2+ currents.

claim: After 100 ms depolarization from -80 to -10 mV, the exocytotic response in control IHCs reaches a maximum amplitude of 22.0 ± 2.9 fF.
source: After 100 ms depolarization, from -80 to -10 mV, the exocytotic response in control IHCs reached a maximum amplitude of 22.0 ± 2.9 fF (n = 11).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: A 40 nm diameter synaptic vesicle corresponds to 37 aF.
source: Considering that a 40 nm diameter synaptic vesicle corresponds to 37 aF (Lenzi et al., 1999), we estimated a RRP size of about 590 vesicles, i.e 33 vesicles per ribbons if we assume a number of 18 ribbons per IHCs.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The RRP size in control IHCs is about 590 vesicles, corresponding to 33 vesicles per ribbon assuming 18 ribbons per IHC.
source: Considering that a 40 nm diameter synaptic vesicle corresponds to 37 aF (Lenzi et al., 1999), we estimated a RRP size of about 590 vesicles, i.e 33 vesicles per ribbons if we assume a number of 18 ribbons per IHCs.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data and cited conversion factor.

claim: The estimated RRP size of 33 vesicles per ribbon fits well with previous findings.
source: This number of RRP vesicles fit well with previous findings (Johnson et al., 2008; Vincent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by comparison with cited previous studies.

claim: In latrunculin-treated IHCs, the exocytotic responses reach 32.4 ± 3.3 fF at 100 ms, significantly larger compared to control IHCs.
source: In latrunculin-treated IHCs, the exocytotic responses reached, at 100 ms, 32.4 ± 3.3 fF (n = 18), a value significantly larger as compared to control IHCs (p<0.05; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The exocytotic response saturates at 90–100 ms in control IHCs but does not show saturation in latrunculin-treated IHCs.
source: Remarkably, while the exocytotic response saturated at 90–100 ms in controls, the response did not show saturation in latrunculin-treated IHCs.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The disruption of F-actin does not affect the steps of vesicle docking and priming but facilitates the replenishment of the RRP.
source: Since the exocytotic response was unchanged for short impulses below 30 ms (Figure 2B), these results suggested that the disruption of F-actin did not affect the steps of vesicle docking and priming but facilitated the replenishment of the RRP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that short impulses are unchanged while longer impulses show facilitation.

claim: In bassoon mutants with abnormal number of anchored ribbons and reduced Ca2+ currents, both short (20 ms) and long (100 ms) impulse activated-exocytosis are affected.
source: In bassoon mutants with abnormal number of anchored ribbons and reduced Ca2+ currents both short (20 ms) and long (100 ms) impulse activated-exocytosis were affected (Jing et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The exocytotic facilitation in latrunculin-treated IHCs is greatly reduced to 21.8 ± 2.5 fF at 100 ms when intracellular Ca2+ buffering is increased with 5 mM EGTA.
source: The exocytotic facilitation in latrunculin-treated IHCs was greatly reduced to 21.8 ± 2.5 fF at 100 ms (n = 7) and comparable to controls (p=0.9) when intracellular Ca2+ buffering was increased with 5 mM EGTA (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The sensitivity of exocytotic facilitation to EGTA suggests a spatial disorganization of the Ca2+ channel clusters in regards to the release sites in latrunculin-treated IHCs.
source: This sensitivity to EGTA suggested a spatial disorganization of the Ca2+ channel clusters in regards to the release sites in latrunculin-treated IHCs, in good agreement with confocal imaging (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the EGTA sensitivity data and confocal imaging results.

claim: Rising the EGTA concentration could affect the extent to which neighboring calcium sources interact and summate to produce a global effect on free calcium.
source: Rising the EGTA concentration could also affect the extent to which neighboring calcium sources interact and summate to produce a global effect on free calcium.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: The synaptic F-actin network acts as a diffusion barrier for synaptic vesicles limiting the access to the site of release.
source: One explanation is that the synaptic F-actin network, in addition to organizing Ca2+ microdomains, also acts as a diffusion barrier for synaptic vesicles limiting the access to the site of release, as suggested in some central synapses (Cingolani and Goda, 2008).
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on inference from the data and cited previous work.

claim: Disruption of F-actin with depolymerising agents facilitates vesicle replenishment of the release sites by increasing the number of available vesicles for docking and priming.
source: Its disruption with depolymerising agents would therefore facilitate vesicle replenishment of the release sites, as shown in a large variety of secretory cells (Malacombe et al., 2006), by increasing the number of available vesicles for docking and priming.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on inference and cited previous work.

claim: A disrupted F-actin could facilitate the diffusion of Ca2+ from its sites of entry and stimulate replenishment.
source: Alternatively, a disrupted F-actin could facilitate the diffusion of Ca2+ from its sites of entry and stimulate replenishment.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative explanation.

claim: Exocytosis triggered by intracellular Ca2+ uncaging shows large facilitation in latrunculin-treated IHCs.
source: To directly test these hypothesis, we studied the effect of F-actin depolimerization on exocytosis triggered by intracellular Ca2+ uncaging, i.e. independently of the activation and the organization of the Ca2+ channels. In these experiments, a large exocytotic facilitation was also observed in latrunculin-treated IHCs (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ uncaging experiments.

claim: The peak exocytotic rate is nearly two fold larger in latrunculin-treated IHCs (25.9 ± 2.7 pF/s) compared to controls (13.7 ± 1.7 pF/s).
source: The peak exocytotic rate, obtained by measuring the first derivative function of the curves in Figure 2C, was nearly two fold larger in latrunculin-treated IHCs as compared to controls (Figure 2D; 25.9 ± 2.7 pF/s (n = 14) and 13.7 ± 1.7 pF/s (n = 16), respectively; p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of Ca2+ uncaging experiments.

claim: The levels of peak intracellular Ca2+ concentration reached upon UV-flash Ca2+ uncaging are similar in control (59 ± 7 µM) and latrunculin-treated IHCs (57 ± 5 µM).
source: The levels of the peak intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]free) reached upon UV-flash Ca2+ uncaging were verified to be similar in control (n = 7) and latrunculin-treated IHCs (n = 5), respectively 59 ± 7 µM and 57 ± 5 µM (p=0.9; Figure 2C-inset).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ measurements using fluorescent indicator.

claim: A synaptic F-actin network controls the diffusion rate of the synaptic vesicles to the sites of release in IHCs.
source: These Ca2+ uncaging experiments again suggested that a synaptic F-actin network controls the diffusion rate of the synaptic vesicles to the sites of release in IHCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Ca2+ uncaging experiments showing facilitation independent of Ca2+ channel effects.

claim: Intracellular hydrostatic pressure influences membrane tension and exocytosis through the F-actin network in mast cells.
source: Furthermore, since intracellular hydrostatic pressure has been suggested to influence membrane tension and exocytosis through the F-actin network in many cell types such as mast cells (Solsona et al., 1998), we probed Ca2+-evoked exocytosis under various intracellular osmotic pressures in auditory IHCs.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Increasing intracellular osmotic pressure from 310 to 390 mOsm with sucrose produces a significant increase in the resting membrane capacitance of IHCs.
source: We first found that increasing intracellular osmotic pressure from 310 to 390 mOsm with sucrose produced a significant increase in the resting membrane capacitance of IHCs.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The resting size of IHCs voltage-clamped at -80 mV for 2 min after break-in is 9.93 ± 0.27 pF at 310 mOsm and 11.10 ± 0.34 pF at 390 mOsm.
source: The resting size of IHCs, voltage-clamped at -80 mV for a period of 2 min after break-in, was 9.93 ± 0.27 pF (n = 11, 310 mOsm) and 11.10 ± 0.34 pF (n = 10, 390 mOsm; p<0.05), respectively.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The augmentation of IHC resting membrane capacitance at high osmotic pressure is about 50 times larger than the size of the RRP evoked by membrane depolarization.
source: This augmentation of the IHC resting membrane capacitance was about 50 times larger than the size of the RRP evoked by membrane depolarization (Figure 2B; RRP = 22 fF).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental measurements.

claim: High intracellular hydrostatic pressure triggers the fusion of a large amount of extrasynaptic vesicles to the plasma membrane.
source: One possible explanation was that high intracellular hydrostatic pressure triggers the fusion of a large amount of extrasynaptic vesicles to the plasma membrane, as previously suggested for Ca2+ uncaging (Vincent et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on inference and cited previous work.

claim: Under intracellular hyperosmotic stress at 390 mOsm, voltage-dependent Ca2+ currents display larger amplitude compared to control conditions at 310 mOsm.
source: Remarkably, in these latter conditions of intracellular hyperosmotic stress at 390 mOsm, voltage-dependent Ca2+ currents displayed larger amplitude (Figure 3A,C) and accelerated activation kinetics as compared to control conditions at 310 mOsm (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Under intracellular hyperosmotic stress at 390 mOsm, voltage-dependent Ca2+ currents display accelerated activation kinetics compared to control conditions at 310 mOsm.
source: Remarkably, in these latter conditions of intracellular hyperosmotic stress at 390 mOsm, voltage-dependent Ca2+ currents displayed larger amplitude (Figure 3A,C) and accelerated activation kinetics as compared to control conditions at 310 mOsm (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: A shift in voltage-dependence of Ca2+ currents toward more negative potentials is observed at 390 mOsm compared to 310 mOsm.
source: A shift in their voltage-dependence toward more negative potentials was also observed (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The hydrostatic pressure effects on Ca2+ currents are no longer visible when IHCs are pre-treated with latrunculin-A.
source: The hydrostatic pressure effects on Ca2+ currents were no longer visible when IHCs were pre-treated with latrunculin-A (Figure 2A, pink line) and were greatly reduced in IHCs lacking otoferlin (Otof-/-; Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The hydrostatic pressure effects on Ca2+ currents are greatly reduced in IHCs lacking otoferlin.
source: The hydrostatic pressure effects on Ca2+ currents were no longer visible when IHCs were pre-treated with latrunculin-A (Figure 2A, pink line) and were greatly reduced in IHCs lacking otoferlin (Otof-/-; Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The Cav1.3 channels of IHCs are mechanosensitive, like the Cav1.2 channels in smooth muscle cells.
source: This indicated that the Cav1.3 channels of IHCs are mechanosensitive, like the Cav1.2 channels in smooth muscle cells (Lyford et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison with cited previous work.

claim: The mechanosensitivity of Cav1.3 channels in IHCs requires an intact synaptic F-actin network and otoferlin.
source: In our study, the sensitivity to membrane tension in IHCs required an intact synaptic F-actin network and otoferlin, a proposed synaptic Ca2+ sensor thought to interact physically with the Cav1.3 II-III loop (Ramakrishnan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing loss of mechanosensitivity with latrunculin-A and in Otof-/- IHCs.

claim: Otoferlin is a proposed synaptic Ca2+ sensor thought to interact physically with the Cav1.3 II-III loop.
source: In our study, the sensitivity to membrane tension in IHCs required an intact synaptic F-actin network and otoferlin, a proposed synaptic Ca2+ sensor thought to interact physically with the Cav1.3 II-III loop (Ramakrishnan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: An increase in Ca2+ current amplitude in low bath hydrostatic pressure (equivalent to increasing intracellular pressure) was reported in dissociated guinea pig vestibular hair cells.
source: Notably, an increase in Ca2+ current amplitude in low bath hydrostatic pressure (equivalent to increasing intracellular pressure) was also reported in dissociated guinea pig vestibular hair cells (Duong Dinh et al., 2009; Haasler et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pressure effects on K+ currents have been shown in guinea-pig IHCs.
source: Although pressure effects on K+ currents have also been shown in guinea-pig IHCs (Kimitsuki, 2013), we don't think that these currents would influence our Ca2+ current measurements since we were working in conditions where most K+ currents are blocked.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study and inference about experimental conditions.

claim: The mechanosensitivity of the Cav1.3 channels is mediated through an intact synaptic F-actin network.
source: Overall, our results suggested here that the mechanosensitivity of the Cav1.3 channels is mediated through an intact synaptic F-actin network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing loss of mechanosensitivity with F-actin disruption.

claim: Exocytosis triggered by voltage-activation of Ca2+ channels from -80 to -10 mV shows maximum facilitation when intracellular pressure is increased from 310 to 390 mOsm.
source: Exocytosis triggered by voltage-activation of Ca2+ channels from -80 to -10 mV (a voltage at which Ca2+ current amplitude is maximum, Figure 3A) also showed maximum facilitation when intracellular pressure was increased from 310 to 390 mOsm (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Exocytosis increases for short impulses (10–20 ms) at 390 mOsm, suggesting that the last steps of vesicle exocytosis (docking, priming and/or fusion) are accelerated.
source: Notably, on the contrary to what observed when disrupting the synaptic F-actin, exocytotis increased for short impulses (10–20 ms) at 390 mOsm (Figure 3F,G), suggesting that the last steps of vesicle  exocytosis  (docking, priming and/or fusion) were here accelerated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that short impulses are affected by osmotic pressure but not by F-actin disruption.

claim: Exocytosis for longer steps up to 90 ms increases from 1.40 ± 0.23 fF/pC at 310 mOsm to 2.58 ± 0.49 fF/pC at 390 mOsm at 50 ms.
source: Exocytosis for longer steps up to 90 ms also increased, from 1.40 ± 0.23 fF/pC (n = 7, 310 mOsm) to 2.58 ± 0.49 fF/pC (n = 5, 390 mOsm; p<0.05) at 50 ms (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The replenishment rate of the RRP is accelerated at 390 mOsm.
source: These latter results suggested that the replenishment rate of the RRP was also accelerated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased exocytosis for longer stimuli.

claim: The facilitation of exocytosis under intracellular hyperosmotic stress appears unrelated to the effects on Ca2+ channels.
source: This facilitation of exocytosis, under intracellular hyperosmotic stress, appeared unrelated to the effects on Ca2+ channels since it was also observed when directly uncaging intracellular Ca2+ (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on Ca2+ uncaging experiments showing facilitation independent of Ca2+ channel activation.

claim: The levels of peak [Ca2+]free reached upon UV-flash Ca2+ uncaging are similar in 310 mOsm (59 ± 7 µM) and 390 mOsm (64 ± 6 µM) conditions.
source: The levels of the peak [Ca2+]free reached upon UV-flash Ca2+ uncaging were verified to be similar in 310 mOsm (n = 7) and 390 mOsm (n = 5) conditions, 59 ± 7 µM and 64 ± 6 µM (p=0.6; Figure 4A-inset).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ measurements using fluorescent indicator.

claim: The strength of exocytotic facilitation is maximal at 390 mOsm and abruptly decreases at 410 mOsm.
source: In these latter conditions of intracellular hyperosmotic stress, the strength of exocytotic facilitation was maximal at 390 mOsm and abruptly decreased at 410 mOsm, a high pressure at which the intrinsic organization of the IHC exocytotic machinery may have been damaged.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements at different osmotic pressures.

claim: At 390 mOsm, the maximum amplitude of the exocytotic response is 1.5 ± 0.15 pF compared to 1.0 ± 0.1 pF in controls at 310 mOsm.
source: At 390 mOsm, the maximum amplitude of the exocytotic response was 1.5 ± 0.15 pF (n = 9) as compared to 1.0 ± 0.1 pF (n = 16) in controls at 310 mOsm (p<0.05; Figure 4A,C).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ uncaging experiments.

claim: The peak exocytotic rate is largely increased at 390 mOsm (25.0 ± 4.5 pF/s) compared to 310 mOsm (13.7 ± 1.7 pF/s).
source: The peak exocytotic rate was largely increased at 390 mOsm as compared to 310 mOsm (25.0 ± 4.5 pF/s (n = 9) and 13.7 ± 1.7 pF/s (n = 16), respectively; p<0.05, Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ uncaging experiments.

claim: The facilitation of exocytosis by high intracellular hydrostatic pressure is not observed in IHCs treated with latrunculin-A.
source: Interestingly, the facilitation of exocytosis by high intracellular hydrostatic pressure was not observed in IHCs treated with latrunculin-A (Figure 2D, pink bars) and in Otof-/- IHCs (Figure 3H and Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements in latrunculin-A treated and Otof-/- IHCs.

claim: The facilitation of exocytosis by high intracellular hydrostatic pressure is not observed in Otof-/- IHCs.
source: Interestingly, the facilitation of exocytosis by high intracellular hydrostatic pressure was not observed in IHCs treated with latrunculin-A (Figure 2D, pink bars) and in Otof-/- IHCs (Figure 3H and Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements in Otof-/- IHCs.

claim: The peak [Ca2+]free reached upon UV-flash Ca2+ uncaging is unchanged in Otof-/- IHCs compared to control IHCs.
source: The peak [Ca2+]free reached upon UV-flash Ca2+ uncaging was unchanged in Otof-/- IHCs as compared to control IHCs (Vincent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The facilitation of exocytosis by high intracellular hydrostatic pressure could be explained by an increased membrane tension that impacts on membrane fusion.
source: Overall, the facilitation of exocytosis by high intracellular hydrostatic pressure could be explained by an increased membrane tension that impacts on membrane fusion (Kozlov and Chernomordik, 2015) but also by an increased vesicular mobility, possibly as the result of reduced molecular crowding and loosened vesicle interactions, accelerating the replenishment rate.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on inference and cited previous work.

claim: The facilitation of exocytosis by high intracellular hydrostatic pressure could be explained by increased vesicular mobility as a result of reduced molecular crowding and loosened vesicle interactions.
source: Overall, the facilitation of exocytosis by high intracellular hydrostatic pressure could be explained by an increased membrane tension that impacts on membrane fusion (Kozlov and Chernomordik, 2015) but also by an increased vesicular mobility, possibly as the result of reduced molecular crowding and loosened vesicle interactions, accelerating the replenishment rate.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on inference.

claim: The mobility of vesicles in pancreatic cells and primary hepatocytes is affected by hydrostatic pressure, a process related to molecular crowding and microfilaments polymerization.
source: In the same way, the mobility of vesicles in pancreatic cells and primary hepatocytes was shown to be affected by hydrostatic pressure, a process related to molecular crowding and microfilaments polymerization (Nunes et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Large intercompartmental osmotic gradients from 289 to 322 mOsmol/kg H2O are present between the perilymphatic and endolymphatic compartments in the cochlea.
source: In the cochlea, large intercompartmental osmotic gradients from 289 to 322 mOsmol/kg H20 are present between the perilymphatic and endolymphatic compartments, respectively (Sterkers et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Osmotic gradients in the cochlea are likely regulated by aquaporins present in outer sulcus cells.
source: These osmotic gradients are likely regulated by aquaporins present in outer sulcus cells (Eckhard et al., 2015) and genetic deletion of aquaporin-4 in mice leads to impaired hearing (Li and Verkman, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic deletion of aquaporin-4 in mice leads to impaired hearing.
source: These osmotic gradients are likely regulated by aquaporins present in outer sulcus cells (Eckhard et al., 2015) and genetic deletion of aquaporin-4 in mice leads to impaired hearing (Li and Verkman, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Osmolarity changes in inner ear fluid compartments have long been suspected to be contributing factors to inner ear disorders such as tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss, inclusive of Menière's disease.
source: Osmolarity changes in these inner fluid compartments have long been suspected to be contributing factors to inner ear disorders such as tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss, inclusive of Menière's disease (Angelborg et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Outer hair cells are mechanically sensitive to extracellular osmotic variation.
source: The outer hair cells, producing the electro-mechanical amplification of sound in the cochlea, have been shown to be mechanically sensitive to extracellular osmotic variation (Dulon, et al., 1987), a factor that greatly influence hearing (Choi and Oghalai, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Osmotic variation greatly influences hearing.
